title: Genoa
wiki_lead:
Genoa is the sixth-largest city in Italy and the capital of the region of Liguria in northern Italy. As of 2026, 566,247 people live within the city's administrative limits. While its metropolitan city has 820,691 inhabitants, more than 1.8 million people live in the wider metropolitan area stretching along the Italian Riviera.
On the Gulf of Genoa in the Ligurian Sea, Genoa has historically been one of the most important ports on the Mediterranean: it is the busiest port in Italy and the Mediterranean Sea and twelfth-busiest in the European Union.
Genoa was the eponymous capital of one of the most powerful maritime republics for over seven centuries, from the 11th century to 1797. Particularly from the 12th century to the 15th century, the city played a leading role in the history of commerce and trade in Europe, becoming one of the largest naval powers of the continent and considered among the wealthiest cities in the world. It was also nicknamed la Superba ("the superb one") by Petrarch due to its glories on the seas and impressive landmarks. The city has hosted massive shipyards and steelworks since the 19th century, and its solid financial sector dates back to the Middle Ages. The Bank of Saint George, founded in 1407, is the oldest known state deposit bank in the world and has played an important role in the city's prosperity since the middle of the 15th century.
The historical centre, or old town, of Genoa is one of the largest and most-densely populated in Europe. Part of it was also inscribed on the World Heritage List (UNESCO) in 2006 as Genoa: Le Strade Nuove and the system of the Palazzi dei Rolli. Genoa's historical city centre is also known for its narrow lanes and streets called caruggi ('alleys'). Genoa is also home to the University of Genoa, which has a history going back to the 15th century, when it was known as Genuense Athenaeum. The city's rich cultural history in art, music and cuisine allowed it to become the 2004 European Capital of Culture. It is the birthplace of Guglielmo Embriaco, Christopher Columbus, Simonetta Vespucci, Andrea Doria, Niccolò Paganini, Giuseppe Mazzini, Pope Benedict XV, Renzo Piano, Fabrizio De André and Grimaldo Canella, founder of the House of Grimaldi, among others.
Genoa, which forms the southern corner of the Milan-Turin-Genoa industrial triangle of Northwest Italy, is one of the country's major economic centres. A number of leading Italian companies are based in the city, including Fincantieri, Leonardo, Ansaldo Energia, Ansaldo STS, Erg, Piaggio Aerospace, Mediterranean Shipping Company and Costa Cruises.

Etymology
The city's modern name may derive from the Latin word genua ([ˈɡe.nu.aː]; singular: genu [ˈɡe.nuː]), meaning 'knees', because of its position at the centre of the Ligurian coastal arch, which was deemed the "knee region" of a "booted leg".
An alternative origin for it is the theonym of Janus, a Roman deity said to have two faces: a fore-turned one and a back-turned one, which was eventually used as a metaphor for the city's two sides (or "faces"): the sea-facing southside and the mountains-facing northside. The Latin word ianua ([ˈjaː.nu.a]) is yet another proposed source of the name, related to Janus's name and meaning 'door' or 'passage' (into the Italian Peninsula). The Latin name oppidum Genua ([ˈop.pi.dum ˈɡe.nu.a]; 'Genoa town') was recorded by Pliny the Elder as part of the Augustan Regio IX Liguria (English: Liguria the Ninth Region).
Finally, the placename might have had an origin in the Etruscan language, specifically in the term Kainua, which meant 'new city'. Such etymology was proposed after the discovery of an Etruscan pottery-sherd inscription that read Kainua; it suggests that the Latin name would have been an alteration of that older Etruscan name, whose original "New City" meaning was lost to the Roman tongue.

As Italy 's principal cargo port, Genoa handled 66.2 million tonnes of goods in 2023, supporting key sectors including container shipping, bulk commodities, and logistics that contribute substantially to national trade and GDP. The city's metropolitan area encompasses diverse terrains from coastal urban zones to inland hills, fostering a economy centered on maritime activities, tourism, and advanced services. Historically, Genoa rose as the core of the Republic of Genoa, a sovereign maritime power from 1099 to 1797 that dominated Mediterranean commerce through innovative banking practices, colonial outposts in the Levant and Black Sea, and naval victories against rivals like Venice and Pisa. This era established Genoa's defining traits: a dense network of fortified palazzi, rolle palaces inscribed as UNESCO sites, and a legacy of seafaring exploration exemplified by native son Christopher Columbus's voyages. The republic's oligarchic governance, blending noble families and merchant guilds, prioritized empirical trade expansion over territorial conquest, yielding causal advantages in financeâsuch as early public debt instrumentsâand shipbuilding that propelled economic resilience amid frequent plagues and wars. In modern times, Genoa's port infrastructure has undergone expansions, including deepened channels and automated terminals, positioning it as the southern gateway for Alpine-Rhine corridors and a hub for EU container traffic despite challenges like bridge collapses and labor disputes. The city proper recorded 562,672 residents as of mid-2024, within a provincial population exceeding 818,000, reflecting demographic shifts driven by immigration offsetting low birth rates. Notable cultural assets include its UNESCO-listed historic center with over 100 medieval churches and the Aquarium, Europe's largest, underscoring Genoa's blend of industrial grit and preserved Renaissance architecture. Controversies have centered on urban decay in peripheral caruggi alleys and environmental impacts from port growth, yet infrastructure investments, such as the new breakwater, signal commitments to sustained maritime primacy.
